Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• Acute onset (today) of right-sided pleuritic chest/back pain, dyspnoea, two episodes of haemoptysis, subjective fever  
• Two-week prodrome of fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance  
• Underlying SLE on methotrexate (immunosuppressed and hypercoagulable)  
• Video exam: pulse 66–74 bpm, normal capillary refill, stable appearance, clear oropharynx, no cervical lymphadenopathy  

Working diagnosis  
Community-acquired pneumonia (high likelihood)—supports: fever, pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, immunosuppression (DDx-rank #1).

Considerations  
• Pulmonary embolism (medium likelihood)—classic triad present; SLE confers clot risk despite normal pulse and no provoking factors.  
• Methotrexate-related pneumonitis/alveolar haemorrhage (medium-low).  
• SLE-related pleuritis or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage (low).  

Management plan  
1. Same-day face-to-face GP review for:  
   • Chest auscultation, full vital signs (BP, RR, Temp, SpO₂)  
   • Consider chest X-ray and baseline bloods (FBC, CRP, D-dimer if PE considered, renal/LFTs).  
2. Empiric oral antibiotic therapy if pneumonia confirmed; withhold until in-person assessment.  
3. Escalate to emergency care if clinical instability noted (tachycardia, hypoxia, hypotension, worsening haemoptysis).  
4. Discuss potential need for CT pulmonary angiography if PE suspected.  
5. Reassure patient regarding low immediate probability of lung cancer; outline plan for follow-up imaging if symptoms persist.

- Patient health goals and priorities:  Relief of breathlessness and clarification of diagnosis; anxiety about lung cancer

- Follow-up and recall appointments scheduled:  Support team to book face-to-face appointment today; further follow-up dependent on findings

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Community-acquired pneumonia – High likelihood: matches acute fever, pleuritic pain, cough with haemoptysis in immunosuppressed host.  
2. Pulmonary embolism – Medium likelihood: pleuritic pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, underlying SLE hypercoagulability; fewer provoking factors and normal pulse lessen probability.  
3. Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis/alveolar haemorrhage – Medium-Low likelihood: temporal association with methotrexate dose; can present with cough and dyspnoea but less commonly abrupt and febrile.
